notes.meaning: God gives Ezekiel a fresh message to deliver against Egypt. He commands the people to weep and howl because a dreadful day of ruin is on its way. The cry expresses the deep terror and grief that will overtake those who mocked God.

The "Day of the LORD" means a special time when God steps in to judge human wickedness and set things right. Here it is described as a dark, cloudy day when nations that opposed God will finally face his justice. People may try to ignore God's warnings, but his day of reckoning arrives right on schedule.

The invading army of Babylon will strike Egypt with the sword, taking its wealth and tearing down its power. The neighboring land of Cush, or Ethiopia, will tremble in agony when it sees Egypt fall, knowing it may be next. All the supports and basic institutions that Egypt trusted in will completely collapse.

Egypt's allies and hired foreign soldiers will fall right alongside her in battle. Nations from across North Africa and other allied fighters shared in Egypt's pride, so they will share in her defeat. Putting our confidence in worldly alliances cannot protect us from God's judgment.

Everyone who props up Egypt will be brought down, and her boastful military power will sink. The destruction will stretch across the entire country, from Migdol in the far north to Syene in the south. No corner of the land will be able to escape God's reach.

Egypt will be left empty and ruined, just like other nations that faced God's judgment before her. Her famous, crowded cities will be turned into piles of rubble. Human achievements and great populations cannot stand when God removes his blessing.

God compares the coming war to a consuming fire that burns across Egypt and destroys all who try to help her. When this happens, the people will finally recognize that the Lord alone is God. Seeing God's judgment shows that nothing in all creation can match his absolute power.

Messengers traveling up the Nile in boats will bring terrifying news of Egypt's collapse to Cush. The people of Cush felt secure because they lived far away, but the panic of judgment will shatter their false sense of safety. God proves that distance cannot hide anyone from his divine purpose.

God names Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, as the man who will carry out this destruction. The bustling crowds and great wealth of Egypt will be wiped out by his army. Even pagan rulers serve as tools in God's hands to accomplish his plans.

The Babylonian army is described as the most ruthless and terrifying force of its day. God brings them into Egypt to draw their swords and cover the fields with the bodies of the dead. God sometimes uses harsh earthly powers to discipline nations that refuse to honor him.

God promises to dry up the canals of the Nile River, which were the lifeblood of Egypt's farming and natural defense. He speaks of handing the country over like sold property into the grasp of cruel invaders. The Lord guarantees that whatever he decrees will certainly take place.

The Lord will destroy the carved idols and false gods worshipped in the great city of Memphis. Egypt will no longer have a native prince of its own to rule the country, and terror will grip every heart. False gods cannot protect their followers when the true God acts.

God will lay waste the regions of southern Egypt, burn the ancient northern capital Zoan, and bring judgment on Thebes. Cities famous for their ancient history and massive temples will be humbled by fire and sword. Earthly glory and long history offer no defense against God's holy anger.

God's wrath will fall upon Pelusium, the heavily fortified border city known as the key defense of Egypt. At the same time, the huge crowds living in Thebes will be cut down. Neither strong military walls nor massive populations can keep out God's judgment.

A blaze of warfare will sweep across Egypt, leaving frontier fortresses writhing in pain and great cities breached. The enemy will strike Memphis boldly in broad daylight without fear of resistance. God shows that no fortification is strong enough to resist his appointed time of judgment.

The young soldiers of On and Pi-beseth, centers of sun worship and idol temples, will be killed in battle. The surviving citizens of those cities will be marched away into exile. Those who rely on false religions will find that their idols cannot save their own children.

The royal city of Tahpanhes will experience a dark day of sorrow when God breaks Egypt's power to rule over other nations. A dark cloud of disaster will cover the city, and its surrounding villages will be dragged away into captivity. True peace comes only when oppressive worldly powers are brought low by God.

God wraps up this part of the message by declaring that these judgments will be carried out with complete justice. Through these terrible events, Egypt and the surrounding nations will finally learn that the Lord alone is God. God's purpose in judgment is to reveal his true power and glory to the world.

God gives Ezekiel a new prophecy with an exact date, just a few months before Jerusalem fell to the Babylonians. The timing was crucial because the people in Jerusalem were still hoping Egypt would come to rescue them. God spoke clearly so his people would stop placing their faith in an unreliable ally.

God announces that he has already broken one of Pharaoh's arms, meaning he crushed Egypt's military might when Babylon defeated them earlier. This broken arm was never properly bandaged or splinted, so Pharaoh cannot lift a sword to fight. When God weakens a proud ruler, no human effort can restore that lost strength.

Because Egypt did not humble itself after the first defeat, the Lord declares that he will break both of Pharaoh's arms. He will shatter the one that was already injured as well as the arm that still seemed strong, knocking the sword straight out of the king's hand. If lesser warnings do not lead people to turn to God, greater judgments will follow.

The Egyptian people will be driven from their homeland and scattered among other nations. God will break up their powerful kingdom and make them live as foreigners in distant countries. Those who trust in earthly security will discover how quickly home and comfort can vanish.

The Lord will give strength to the king of Babylon and place his own divine sword in the conqueror's hands. At the same time, Pharaoh will be left broken and helpless, groaning like a soldier who has received a fatal wound. God decides which leaders rise and which leaders fall.

Pharaoh's arms will fall completely limp while Babylon's arms are strengthened by God to swing the sword against Egypt. When this happens, everyone will see that Nebuchadnezzar's victory came entirely from the Lord. World leaders only have the power that God permits them to use.

God repeats that he will scatter the people of Egypt into exile across other lands. Through this scattering and loss of their nation, they will finally know that the Lord is the true and living God. God uses even deep suffering to teach people the truth about who he is.
